https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/insu.title: Insulate Britain protester married to Transport for London boss
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/insu.text:
An Insulate Britain protester who has been arrested on numerous occasions for blocking the M25 is married to a Transport for London boss, it emerged last night.
Cathy Eastburn, a Cambridge University philosophy graduate, lives with Benedict Plowden, 58, in South London and she has allowed David McKenny, 38, a fellow activist, to stay at the home, The Sun said.
Greg Smith, a Conservative MP and member of the transport select committee, told the newspaper: “Insulate Britain has caused untold misery for individuals and businesses over recent weeks. It is an absolute kick in the teeth that someone senior in TfL — an arm of the British state — has been harbouring them in their house. This is unacceptable.
“It is unbelievable that someone in TfL — who have themselves been victim to these extremists — have been looking after these extremists in luxury.”
Last month The Sunday Times disclosed that Eastburn, 54, a musician, is one of Britain’s most prolific climate change activists, having been arrested at least 12 times in three years.
During the M25 protests she was arrested four times in nine days. She was released without charge each time.
In 2019 she was arrested twice in London protesting for Extinction Rebellion by gluing herself to a hotel and a DLR train.
Her first known involvement in the Insulate Britain protests was on September 15 when she was pictured on the M25 near Dartford, Kent.
The Sun said that her out-of-office reply to emails says: “If you’re reading this, it is because I have been arrested and possibly put in prison on remand.”
Transport for London said that Plowden would be stepping down after 20 years at the organisation. A spokesman said: “We do not comment on the activities of the families of our staff. Ben Plowden has been a dedicated servant of London for many years — including playing a pivotal role in ensuring the London 2012 Games were a success.
“He decided several weeks ago that he will be leaving TfL at the end of October to pursue other opportunities.”

https://www.thetimes.com/culture/books/a.title: My culture fix: Jack Whitehall
https://www.thetimes.com/culture/books/a.text:
My favourite author or bookEvelyn Waugh. Decline and Fall holds a special place in my heart because I was lucky enough to get to be a part of bringing it to television and it remains one of my favourite books. I also love Scoop, Brideshead Revisited — even lesser-known novels such as The Loved One are fantastic. In his early comic works I can’t get enough of his wicked sense of humour and deranged cast of characters.
The book I’m readingDavid Nicholls’s The Understudy. I am a bit obsessed with David Nicholls — I started with Us and now I’m working my way back through his canon. I’ll soon have to resort to reading essays he wrote at school.
The book I wish I had writtenSteve Martin’s Born Standing Up: A Comic’s Life. The benchmark in terms of stand-up autobiography.
The book I couldn’t finishJamie Redknapp’s Me, Family and the Making of a Footballer. It was just too moving. I kept having to put it down because I was an emotional mess. Who knew that anecdotes about going out on the lash with Phil Babb and Stig Inge Bjornebye after the 1995 League Cup final could move a grown man to tears.
The book I’m ashamed I haven’t read My dad Michael Whitehall’s Shark-Infested Waters: Tales of an Actors’ Agent. I only haven’t read it because it’s a memoir full of stories I’ve heard a million times before. For the past 33 years I have essentially been trapped inside its audiobook.
My favourite filmIt has to be Withnail and I. It’s my barometer for whether I’m going to truly like a person. Especially with Americans: the Withnail test. If they like that movie and aren’t appalled by Uncle Monty and Danny then we can be friends.
My favourite playAlan Bennett is a hero of mine. I put on my own performance of Habeas Corpus when I was at school and played a randy vicar — I think it set the tone for the subtle performances I have gone on to be associated with as an actor. The History Boys was a significant moment for me as a theatregoer, watching Richard Griffiths in his pomp commanding a stage. I’d never experienced a play like it and ended up seeing it about five times.
The box set I’m hooked onSuccession. Rewatching it ahead of the series launch. The skill of the writers and actors involved to make you so invested in characters that are that deplorable is amazing. Every performance is pitch perfect.
My favourite TV seriesThe Office. Ricky Gervais and Stephen Merchant’s masterpiece is still my go-to if I need cheering up. It’s so much more than a sitcom — it literally influenced the entire sense of humour for a generation. All these years later my friends and I will send each other YouTube clips from old episodes and quote it in conversation.
The last TV programme that made me cry I’m a big crier and can be set off by anything. I cried at an old episode of Come Dine with Me the other day because a housewife from Princes Risborough was brutally underscored for her Indian banquet.
The lyric I wish I’d written“Swag, swag, swag on you./ Chillin’ by the fire while we eatin’ fondue,” from Justin Bieber’s Boyfriend. As a keen skier and fan of Alpine cuisine this kind of lyricism hit all the right notes for me. This song was the moment I became a Belieber. Until that point I’d be a Bielathiest.
The song that saved meShaggy’s It Wasn’t Me. Many a time I have been caught red-handed, although admittedly not “banging on the bathroom floor”, and had to echo the words of Mr Lover Lover himself.
The instrument I playedRecorder is the only instrument I played, although I hasten to add that it’s not one I mastered. I feel as if my lack of interest in putting in the hard graft has been vindicated since you seldom go to a gig or festival these days and see anyone playing one on stage.
The instrument I wish I’d learntThe bongo drums. Nothing can clear a room at a house party like cracking those out. If guests are outstaying their welcome and you’re yearning for an early night, bongos are the only surefire way to get everyone heading for their coats.
The music that cheers me upDisney soundtracks — I love a bit of The Little Mermaid or the ultimate musical self-help ballad Hakuna Matata. I found an album of instrumental versions recorded by an orchestra. It’s great because you can play it whenever you want and not get judged, since to the casual observer it sounds as if you’re listening to grown-up classical music and not a singing warthog.
If I could own one painting it would be . . .The defaced version of Whistler’s Mother from the first Mr Bean movie.
The place I feel happiestI spend a lot of time in the bath. I actually do quite a lot of work from it. A bit like Churchill. Although to be fair he was writing some of the most powerful speeches of the 20th century — the majority of my “work” is concocting amusing topical observations in under 280 characters or adding dick jokes to scripts.
I’m having a fantasy dinner party, I’ll invite these artists and authors . . .My dad, Michael. Then, just for a laugh, Meghan Markle, Ken Livingstone, Jeremy Corbyn, maybe that student that petitioned to pull down the statue of Winston Churchill and a couple of Extinction Rebellion glued to my dad’s chair. I say chair, it might be fun to do the dinner party in a Wagamama so Michael has to be on a communal bench near members of the public (if anything, even more distressing for him than my guest list), then we sit back and enjoy the show.
And I’ll put on this music . . .We probably won’t need it but if we can’t get a reaction out of him after they’ve delivered the starters (which could come after the mains seeing as we’re at Wagamama, possibly the thing to set him off), the rewritten version of Jerusalem or any popular music recorded after about 1981.
The movie that I’m looking forward to Last Night in Soho. I love everything Edgar Wright does and the trailer for this next offering looks great.
I wasted an evening watching . . .I think in lockdown I may have completed the entire series of Premier League Years on Sky Sports — and that felt like a very poor way of spending my time. I could have learnt a language. Still, it was quite nostalgic to remember happier times pre-pandemic when Arsenal won titles, Man City were skint and Tottenham were a sort of physical comedy troupe (some things never change). It was interesting to discover that Jamie Redknapp did actually have a career prior to becoming a writer/men’s footwear model.
The film I walked out onI don’t tend to walk out on anything. I can watch a film and hate it but still stick it out to the end. I’ve had enough walkouts at the Edinburgh festival from my own shows to know how demoralising it is for a performer. I couldn’t inflict that on anyone else.
OverratedI actually think Beethoven’s First is really overrated.
UnderratedThe second Beethoven where the dog has a litter of puppies. Classic.How to Survive Family Holidays by Jack Whitehall with Hilary and Michael Whitehall is out now, published by Sphere; £18.99

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/insu.title: Drivers drag Insulate Britain protesters off the road
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/insu.subtitle: Altercation hours after jail threat as group breach injunction for third time
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/insu.text:
Paramedics joined drivers to drag Insulate Britain demonstrators off a busy road yesterday as the group defied government attempts to stop the protests.
A furious woman berated protesters blocking the Blackwall Tunnel in London after telling them that she was trying to visit her mother in hospital in Canterbury. She wept as she asked them, “How can you be so selfish?”.
Insulate Britain caused hours of disruption when they blocked roads yesterday morning at Wandsworth Bridge, Hanger Lane and Arnos Grove in the capital. By midday police had arrested 38 of the 54 protesters from the Extinction Rebellion splinter group who took part.
The Metropolitan Police said that all roads were clear at 12.20pm.
Hours earlier the government had been granted an injunction against all activity that obstructs traffic and access to motorways and A-roads in and around London.
The injunction came into force on Sunday and its terms mean that protesters who breach it are likely to be found in contempt of court, facing imprisonment and unlimited fines.
However, the injunction did not cover the roads blocked yesterday, a spokeswoman for National Highways told The Times. “The injunction only covered roads on the strategic road network linked to the M25 in the southeast,” she said. “The roads impacted today are under the management of Transport for London and therefore not part of the strategic road network.”
Video footage showed a paramedic crew joining drivers in pulling the activists off the road at Wandsworth Bridge, with no police in sight.
In a clip shared by LBC, a woman pleaded with protesters at the Blackwall Tunnel to move, saying that she needed to see her mother in hospital. She told them: “We all believe in what you’re doing but I just need to get to my mum . . . everybody agrees with you.”
Asked why they were still blocking roads, an activist said: “No one is doing anything.” The woman replied: “That’s not my fault! And my mum is the one in an ambulance on the way to hospital!”
Roger Hallam, a co-founder of Extinction Rebellion who is behind Insulate Britain, said he would have refused to move for the woman or even for an ambulance carrying someone who was dying. He told the London Economic podcast: “What we’re talking about is the loss of people’s pensions in the next ten years, the loss of people’s incomes, the mass migration of hundreds of millions . . . we’re talking about the biggest crime in human history imposed by the rich against the global poor.”
The latest injunction bans the damaging of road surfaces and infrastructure and prohibits activists from gluing themselves to the road or abandoning vehicles.
A spokesman for Insulate Britain, however, said that they did not believe that the injunction would apply. He said: “Our understanding is that the injunction has to specify which roads in order to be active.”
The protesters sat down sat down on the A102 near the tunnel in east London at about 8.30am, causing a long tailback.
As they assembled, a man waiting at the traffic lights attempted to drive his van around them but ended up slowly driving into one of the activists before reversing.
Insulate Britain, which is demanding that the government pay for all homes in the country to be insulated by 2030, has brought roads and motorways to a standstill with 11 protests in less than three weeks. About 450 arrests have been made so far.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.title: Joanna Lumley on Ab Fab, political correctness and why she’s an eco‑queen
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.text:
Joanna Lumley beams when I mention the Queen’s recent swipe at world leaders’ attitude to climate change. “It’s really irritating when they talk, but they don’t do,” Her Majesty is reported to have said.
“Isn’t that terrific?” Lumley says in her inimitable, breathy, daughter-of-the-Raj tones (she was born in India and has described herself as an army brat). “We’re much, much closer to disaster than we think and we want to see something happening now, not all these people rubbing their chins and having a committee meeting and presenting minutes and back-slapping — ‘Well, we lead the world in this . . . blah blah blah.’ We don’t want to hear about that! We want to hear what the future is.”
Now 75, Lumley became a star to her boomer peers as Purdey in The New Avengers, before entrancing the next generation as sozzled Patsy in Absolutely Fabulous. “But Ab Fab was an extremely long time ago,” she points out. Today, she says she is recognised mostly for the numerous travel documentaries she presents. Yet her acting skills have just as frequently been put to superb use in her impassioned speeches for the many campaigns she has adopted — be it pushing for the right of Gurkha veterans to settle in Britain (successful) or for a £175 million Garden Bridge across the Thames (flop).
Her favourite cause, however, has long been animal welfare (she has been vegetarian since the 1970s). Now this has overlapped with fighting climate change. You really don’t want Lumley to think you’re not an eco-warrior, as I discover when I say — purely as devil’s advocate — perhaps the battle’s already lost and any action we take is too little too late.
“It’s never too late! You are just choosing not to hear,” she reprimands me, and I feel as if I’ve been beaten up by a lily.
Lumley’s talking on Zoom from the home in Stockwell, south London, where she lives with her second husband, the conductor Stephen Barlow. The walls are plastered with splendid art and she looks as preternaturally young and glamorous as ever with brilliant white teeth and a flattering, long blonde bob in keeping with her belief that, “Actors have got to keep a goodish, adaptable shape, you’ve got to get your hair cut or dyed for a part” and that Botox is “entirely up to you”.
Last time we spoke, she scoffed at the idea of being felled by Covid. “I’m not vulnerable. I’m not an ill person.” Wondering about the secret of her extraordinary constitution (she eats very little, which may help, and smokes, which can’t) is, however, very much to detract from the seriousness of the subject at hand, the documentary Joanna Lumley and the Human Swan, which will be shown on ITV next week to coincide with Cop26. It shows Lumley following the “human swan”, the Australian climate activist Sacha Dench, on her green-powered paramotor flight (a bit like a paraglider powered by an electric fan) around Britain’s coast witnessing damage caused by climate change, but also visiting projects seeking solutions, such as an aeroponic farm that grows food vertically in shipping containers to reduce food miles.
Filming had wrapped when last month Dench was in a mid-air collision with her support pilot Dan Burton. Burton died; Dench is in hospital with “life-changing” injuries.
“As soon as this tragedy happened, our sense was ‘back away’ [from broadcasting it],” Lumley says. “But Dan’s brave, brave family said, ‘Please! This is what it’s for’ and Sacha sent a message through her team from her hospital bed, saying, ‘For goodness sake show this film, this is why we were doing it.’ It was hard to take the news on board, knowing how skilful they are. Like mountaineers, they always put safety first. They went through the checklist before every single flight.”
At one point in the film, with characteristic gumption Lumley follows Dench over Dover’s eroded cliffs in a microlight. “The director said, ‘It would look so great,’ and I said, ‘I’m sorry if it’s spoiling it but I’m really not doing this.’ And then Sacha said, ‘I’d really love you to see the cliffs close up,’ and I said . . .” She affects a weedy voice, “ ‘OK, Sacha.’ But once we got up it was thrilling. Vertigo scares me but being in that little, feather thing spinning around didn’t frighten me.”
It’s eye-catching stuff but the terrible denouement makes you wonder about ends justifying means. What does Lumley think about Insulate Britain? She looks blank. “I only came back from Paris yesterday afternoon, so I’ve missed a lot.” I give a brief summary of the eco-activists blocking the M25.
“Suffragettes chained themselves to railings,” Lumley says thoughtfully. “It’s very difficult. I’m not that kind of demonstrator, so I wouldn’t join them but I absolutely understand that sense of inarticulacy where you cannot get the government to listen, because it will go into another committee meeting and say, ‘Thank you so much for this kind comment, we’re going to think hard, lessons will be learnt.’
“You can understand why people get so infuriated they’re driven to do these difficult and horrible things to draw attention to themselves.” She mentions the anti-nuclear protesters camping at Greenham Common in the 1980s and the Czech students who in 2003 self-immolated in protest at the country’s regime. “That’s what Extinction Rebellion are doing.”
What about the ambulances stuck at the blockade, the woman who couldn’t reach her sick mother in hospital? “Sometimes these huge gestures invariably have awful, sad side effects. It’s massively irritating to the people who can’t get to work but you think, ‘How bad is the state of the planet?’ and the answer is very bad. So how else are we going to jolt people, governments, countries into thinking about that seriously?”
Lumley charmed Boris Johnson when he was the mayor of London during the Garden Bridge campaign, persuading him to put up £43 million of public money on the ultimately aborted project. She said then that she had known him since he was four when she had her portrait painted by his mother. Couldn’t she put a word in before Cop26? “It turns out I didn’t meet him aged four, it was one of his baby brothers, this was 1971 and there was a little blond, stocky boy and Boris must have been about seven. So I don’t have any particular access.”
She’s often asked if she’d stand for parliament, but experience has disillusioned her. “Sometimes it’s better to be outside and to rattle tins because once you start fossicking your way into governments and quangos and departments it all slows to a grinding halt, nothing gets done like that,” she says, clapping her hands briskly.
In any case, she says, she’d have to stand as an independent. “And precious few of them are elected. The only party I’ve ever given money to are the Greens because I wanted to have one in parliament. Now do we have six, seven?” No, still only one. “In the western world, profit and this idea of moving forward always come first,” she says disgustedly. “Most people don’t want to move forward, we just want things to be all right now. As an actor I never wanted to rise to the top of the tree and win Oscars, I just wanted to act well and be proud of my work. But there’s this idea of, we’ve got to keep on getting more, changing your phone. We’ve all been whipped into thinking that whatever happened yesterday is old-fashioned.”
She’s still Tiggerish that Cop26 will mark a turning point. “It’s the most important meeting the world has ever seen.” So is she going? “No, I can’t. I’ll be filming in Rome.” This, of course, is exactly the kind of celebrity double standard detractors seize on gleefully. “Yes, yes, I know, like people saying Emma Thompson flew over to join Extinction Rebellion. But they’re the people who do nothing.” I’d raised an eyebrow during the Swan documentary at Lumley following Dench’s progress by road. “All the cars we drove were electric. Anywhere we fly for filming, we carbon offset.”
But not everyone can afford to carbon offset. “Think of the war! A lot of people had money in the war, a lot of people didn’t. We can’t keep saying, ‘Other people are doing this and I couldn’t give a damn.’ It’s the way of envy and jealousy.” Fundamentally, Lumley continues, we’re all going to have to make many sacrifices, especially when it comes to holidays. “We only now understand what it means to fly. In the 1950s it was ‘Up, up and away’ and ‘Would you like a Martini, madam?’ and people smoking and saying, ‘This is jolly nice.’ We can’t do any of that now. We have to understand it’s a different world.”
It’s jolting hearing this pronouncement from the woman who — as Patsy — was the poster girl for the self-indulgent 1990s. “I’m your mother’s age, darling, I didn’t live Patsy, I acted her,” Lumley says. True, but Ab Fab summed up that era’s thoughtless hedonism. Recently, its creator Jennifer Saunders said the show could never be aired today “because everything is sensitive”. Lumley hadn’t heard this, but agrees. “It was so fabulously politically incorrect. Everything they did is frowned on now. Patsy lighting four cigarettes simultaneously, they laughed at that then, now they’d say, ‘That’s awful!’ But I have to say I meet people every day who say, I was [the square daughter] Saffy and my mother was [Saunders’s daffy, selfish] Edina.”
Lumley doesn’t discuss eco matters with her two teenage granddaughters from her only child Jamie, the result of her youthful affair with a photographer. Given that they live in Scotland she has hardly seen them in 18 months. “I hope I’m light with them. I don’t lecture. They’re responsible and lovely girls.”
Her own lockdown passed in a blur of recording audiobooks and radio plays, then — once safety protocols were established — filming dramas and documentaries. She has barely noticed restrictions lifting because she’s been so busy working. “No socialising! No time.”
And no time to waste on saving the planet. “Don’t be too downhearted but make sure you’re doing something now,” she instructs me. “It’s no good saying, ‘Other people are doing it so I needn’t,’ or, ‘It all looks so ghastly, what could one person do?’ ” With a grin, Lumley adds: “I’m quite hearty, clapping hands, ‘Come on, gang, let’s do it!’ I know this Pollyanna-ish attitude can be repellent. But we have got to put vigour into this. We can’t just go on munching away like a caterpillar, thinking [resources] will go on for ever and it’s not our fault. We’ll soon be dead in a heartbeat.”Joanna Lumley and the Human Swan is on ITV at 9pm on November 1

https://www.thetimes.com/article/cop26-g.title: Extinction Rebellion, demos and disruption — Cop26 security challenges
https://www.thetimes.com/article/cop26-g.text:
Cop26 will make Glasgow the world’s most high-value terror target next week with more than 100 heads of state attending the summit. A ring of steel is being erected around the conference site on the north bank of the Clyde, which includes the SSE Hydro and the Scottish Event Campus.As well as guarding against lethal threats, security forces will have to manage potential disruption from climate change protesters. A cat-and-mouse game is under way between activists who want to disrupt the UN climate change summit and police who are determined to stop them in their tracks.
Although a range of potential disorders is possible, from anarchists to single-issue protests against specific heads of state, the main attention will be focused on environmental campaigners.
Extinction Rebellion has warned ministers they should be “very worried” about the planned programme of “targeted disruption” and non-violent direct action. “The UK government’s track record shows they are not taking climate change as seriously as the science is demanding,” said Myke Hall, the group’s Scottish spokesman. “We are unwilling to put up with that any longer.”
● What is Cop26 and why is the climate change conference so important?● Could Cop26 affect Nicola Sturgeon’s dream of Scottish independence?● The Cambo oil field is no barrel of laughs for Nicola Sturgeon
Hall, 34, a Glasgow-based writer and activist, insisted that inconveniencing commuters and world leaders was a price worth paying. “We don’t want to add further disruption into ordinary peoples’ lives, but we are compelled by the inaction of governments, which is bound to create far more disruption when the effects of the climate catastrophe are felt,” he said. “A million plant and animal species are at risk of extinction and the failure of the governments involved is a crime against humanity.”
Security experts say the group has the potential to humiliate the UK government internationally. “If they managed to disrupt the event itself, that would steal the show,” said Dr Tim Wilson, the director of the Handa Centre for the Study of Terrorism and Political Violence at the University of St Andrews. “From a policing point of view Cop26 can be viewed almost as a kind of perfect storm. Historically, most protests are in the city centre, but when you start dispersing things — as social media allows you to do — you can organise in a much more agile kind of way, which presents a greater public order challenge.”
He and Dr Steve Hewitt, an expert in counterterrorism at the University of Birmingham, are convinced that police and the security services will have infiltrated Extinction Rebellion and other groups. “It is a much more effective tactic than simply intercepting communications,” he said.
He pointed to the 2010 G20 summit in Toronto where it later emerged that at least 12 undercover officers infiltrated protest organisations.
Police Scotland insists its approach to protests will be “welcoming, friendly and proportionate”, while stressing there would be “low tolerance” for disruption of motorways and transport routes.
“If it’s a main route, if it involves movement plans for the world leaders, if it involves major disruption to the life of the city, then we will move in and, if the protesters won’t move, we will remove them,” said Deputy Chief Constable Will Kerr.
Hall disclosed that they had created clusters of “self-organising” activist cells to minimise infiltration. “Our decentralised model is what has allowed us to achieve so much in such a short time,” he said.
Glasgow is bracing itself for the largest demonstrations seen in Scotland since protests against the Iraq war in 2003. Up to 150,000 people are expected to take to the streets on Saturday, November 6, which has been designated as the Global Day for Climate Justice.
“We have a unique, once-in-a-lifetime opportunity for people in Scotland to take action on a world stage,” said Luke Henderson of the Cop26 Coalition. “We will never again have global leaders in Scotland on this scale and at such a critical time in history.”
The coalition is made up of dozens of groups, including charities, trade unions, faith groups and environmental campaigners.
Promoting the march, which will start at Kelvingrove Park at midday before winding its way towards Glasgow Green, the coalition states: “Justice won’t be handed to us by world leaders or delivered by corporations.”
One group of activists are planning to walk to the demo from Dunbar, while others will have marched from Cornwall. Some plan to arrive after walking and sailing more than 1,000 miles from Sweden on what has been called the Pilgrim’s Walk for the Future. Hundreds more will join the protest by bicycle, as cyclists from Glasgow and further afield converge in an event called Pedal on Cop26. More than two million people are expected to take part in solidarity demonstrations in cities around the globe.
Businesses in the centre of Glasgow are bracing themselves for the protests and the possibility that events take a violent turn. “We are anticipating significant protests, we know that is coming,” said Stuart Patrick, the chief executive of the city’s chamber of commerce. The prospect of spontaneous disruption from groups such as Extinction Rebellion could not come at a worse time for businesses, he said. “Glasgow has taken a pretty heavy pasting during the pandemic,” he said. “We are not wildly enthusiastic about protests that will damage their prospects further.
“I fully understand the rights of those protesting and have no issue with that,” Patrick said. “The question we have is: what are the rights of businesses to respond and what support will they get from the authorities in responding to protests, especially if they go beyond the acceptable norms and involve damaging or invading property?”
At the G20 event in Toronto in 2010 more than 40 shops were targeted by violent protesters.
Hewitt expects the 10,000 police officers who will patrol the city daily to adopt a robust approach. “Extinction Rebellion disrupting commuters in London is very different to protests where you will have world leaders and delegates at a major international event,” he said.
It was announced in the summer that a new digital information hub aimed at helping Glasgow businesses to prepare for the summit would be launched by the state-funded Scottish Business Resilience Centre.
Assistant chief constable Bernard Higgins said: “Police Scotland officers and staff will continue to work in association with the UK government and other partners to support the delivery of external communication and engagement to ensure people and businesses are able to plan ahead for any potential disruption.”
Concerns have been raised that bringing world leaders and hundreds of thousands of protesters to Scotland’s largest urban centre will spark a surge in Covid cases.
The UK issued an 11th-hour quarantine waiver to ministers from “red list” countries after fears that delegations could be severely curtailed. After a formal complaint from Latin American nations, ministers plus two staff will be exempted from hotel quarantine. Other delegates from red-list countries will still have to quarantine, including technical negotiators and observers from non-governmental organisations.
However, Linda Bauld, a professor at the University of Edinburgh, feared the event could spark a fresh wave of infections. “We have a reservoir of infection in this country and it’s largely in teenagers, and I think that’s the bit of the jigsaw which is really causing big problems at the moment because of course those cases are seeping through now to older age groups,” she said. “I am worried about a Glaswegian spike, and I’m not worried just about Glasgow. The central belt is interconnected and we’re seeing declines here, but we may not be able to hang on to those gains. We’re trying to open up and everything’s trying to operate more normally.”
About 2,500 cases among Scotland football fans were linked to the Euro 2020 championship early in the summer and the nation experienced a new peak in rates of the disease within days of the bigger matches. More than 550 people tested positive for Covid-19 after attending the TRNSMT music festival on Glasgow Green last month, which was attended by 50,000 people.
Cornwall experienced a rise in cases after the G7 summit in June, although Downing Street denied the meeting of government leaders was responsible. Delegates and members of the public will not have to show vaccine certification before entering events at the main Cop26 campus arena at the Scottish Exhibition Centre.
Alok Sharma, the MP who will act as the summit’s president, insisted sensible precautions would be in place: “We are working tirelessly with all our partners, including the Scottish government and the UN, to ensure an inclusive, accessible and safe summit in Glasgow with a comprehensive set of Covid mitigation measures.
“This includes an offer from the UK government to fund the required quarantine hotel stays for registered delegates arriving from red-list areas and to vaccinate accredited delegates who would be unable otherwise to get vaccinated.”
Sections of Scotland’s busiest motorway look set to be closed during the conference, causing potential disruption for commuters.
President Biden will be staying in Edinburgh during the summit, prompting suggestions that parts of the M8, which links Scotland’s two biggest cities, will be closed to the public to ensure the safe transport of world leaders.
Police Scotland is understood to have gathered intelligence about planned protests near junction 19 at Anderston, where leaders and delegates arriving by car will be escorted off the motorway and on to the Clydeside Expressway, which will be reserved solely for conference traffic during the event.
Sources claim drivers should expect delays on the M8 on November 1 and 2 if temporary restrictions are introduced. “This may include around roadworks at the Woodside viaduct, between junctions 16 and 17, where four lanes are reduced to two,” they said. “There are security concerns about having to move VIPs through slow-moving traffic.”
Neil Greig, the director of policy and research with IAM RoadSmart (formerly the Institute of Advanced Motorists), said: “The suggestion that delays and closures could extend right along the M8 to Edinburgh are a huge potential nightmare for anyone trying to go about their business during Cop26.
“It looks as if the entire central belt could become a no-go area at times, with implications for deliveries, appointments and emergency services. The irony will not be lost on drivers sitting fuming in delays that their emissions will be contributing to the very problem that the conference is trying to solve.”
Edinburgh council said that it would be “encouraging people to plan ahead, consider how and if they need to travel and to avoid peak times if possible”.
Adam McVey, the leader of Edinburgh city council, said: “We’re expecting it to be busy right across the central belt, including here in Edinburgh.”
A number of roads in and around Glasgow, including the Clydeside Expressway, Finnieston Quay, Congress Road and Lancefield Quay, will be closed to motorists during the conference and its build-up.
A spokesman for Get Ready Glasgow said: “Cop26 will be unlike any other major event that Glasgow has hosted. It will create a unique set of challenges for our travel network.
“It’s expected it will have an impact on travel across central Scotland. The best ways to keep moving are to: use our maps to plan alternative routes; allow more time for your journey; leave the car at home and use public transport; or walk or cycle where possible.”
Assistant Chief Constable Bernard Higgins added: “Delivering such a complex event as Cop26 means that some security road closures and restrictions may be needed in other areas of the country to facilitate the safety and security of world leaders, heads of state, delegates and local residents.
“We will work with partners to minimise local disruption and communicate in advance any road closures or diversions that are put in place, to allow for people to forward plan their own journeys.”
● Cop stands for “conference of the parties”. The event is a United Nations summit on combating climate change.
● The first Cop was held in Berlin in 1995. Since then it has been held in cities all over the world, the most recent being Madrid in 2019.
● The Glasgow summit will start on October 31 and run for two weeks, finishing on November 12.
● It was supposed to take place last year, but was delayed due to the pandemic.
● Negotiators will largely spend the fortnight talking behind closed doors, occasionally sharing updates on their progress.
● World leaders will fly in to attend high-level talks and hold press conferences; charities and environmental groups will chair panel discussions and talk to the media; and business leaders will tour the halls pitching their companies’ climate ideas.
● The most important result of the summit will be the number of countries who pledge to reach net zero by 2050.
● More than 10,000 police officers from across the country will take part in one of the largest policing operations seen in the UK when world leaders come to Glasgow on November 1 and 2.
● The area around the Scottish Event Campus (SEC) on the banks of the Clyde in Glasgow has been locked down, with a high-security fence being erected to guard against attacks by terrorists or violent protesters.
● Extra security measures have been introduced where the partition crosses roads to prevent vehicle attacks, alongside a network of temporary road closures and restrictions.
● Armed officers and search dogs will patrol the city’s underground and overground rail networks for the duration of the two-week UN event.
● Specialist police divers and officers, using cameras that can capture underwater footage, will be patrolling the Clyde and its banks.
● The army has been brought in to assist with security, while UN troops will be on duty inside the main conference area.
■ 30,000 delegates will make their way to Glasgow.
■ 10,000 police officers from across Scotland and the UK will be on patrol in Glasgow daily during the summit.
■ 197 countries will be included in the talks and most will be represented by their head of state.
■ 150,000 marchers are expected to take to the streets of Glasgow to demand climate justice on November 6.
■ 1 extra hour for drinking granted by the Glasgow Licensing Board to bars and restaurants for the duration of the summit.

https://www.thetimes.com/article/cop26-p.title: Cop26: Police braced for ‘messy’ face-offs with protesters
https://www.thetimes.com/article/cop26-p.text:
“Messy” confrontations are expected at Cop26 as officers “physically engage” with activists trying to disrupt world leaders’ motorcades, the chief constable of Police Scotland has said.
Iain Livingstone said that his officers would use “robust” policing to stop those intent on causing chaos during the conference, which starts tomorrow.
Livingstone said at a briefing that world leaders and others involved in Cop26 would be moving around the city. “There may well be attempts to disrupt or to prevent some of those movements,” he said. “We are going to be doing everything we can to prevent that.
“We will take robust measures. It is absolutely crucial that world leaders can attend so that the conference actually takes place. I am confident that we will be able to deal with whatever arises. But I am expecting challenges.”
“Protest removal teams” were trained and prepared to use physical engagement, Livingstone said. “At times, and I’ve been very clear to the first minister on this . . . and to UK ministers, it may well look quite messy.
“Robust measures will mean physical engagement with protesters.”
A “ring of steel” has been erected around the conference site on the north bank of the Clyde, which includes the SSE Hydro and the Scottish Event Campus. Although many sources of disruption are possible, from anarchists to protests against specific heads of state, attention will be on environmental activists, some of whom have said they will create “deliberate disruption”.
Extinction Rebellion has promised non-violent direct action to grab headlines when world leaders arrive, saying that its activists expect to be arrested.
Greta Thunberg joined activists yesterday at a protest in London to chant “we are unstoppable, another world is possible”. The activists called on banks to stop insuring fossil fuel extraction, but police had to intervene as members of the media rushed to take photographs of Thunberg, 18.
Bad weather has caused chaos in Scotland on the eve of the conference. Some people were told to leave their homes to escape life-threatening floods. A major incident was declared in the Borders town of Hawick as the River Teviot threatened to burst its banks. The Scottish Environment Protection Agency said that 500 homes and businesses were at risk.
Heavy rain battered Glasgow on Wednesday evening and Thursday morning, flooding roads and forcing operators to cancel rail services. Network Rail said there would be speed limits and reduced services on some routes, and disruption to the west coast mainline. Travel between Glasgow and Edinburgh should be avoided unless “absolutely necessary”.
More downpours are forecast before Cop26 begins tomorrow, potentially disrupting travel to and around the conference. The Met Office has given warnings for heavy rain across southern Scotland and Cumbria, where there will be “danger to life from fast-flowing or deep floodwater”.

https://www.thetimes.com/business-money/.title: Inside the Amazon tribe fighting deforestation: ‘This is war’
https://www.thetimes.com/business-money/.text:
The children tumble from the trees into the igarapé, or forest brook, sending up beads of water. Fingers of sunlight break through the patchwork-green canopy overhead, illuminating them. A cobalt-winged butterfly flits past, mesmerising in its brilliance.
Drying off quickly in the hot Amazon sun, the youngsters scramble up a muddy path to their village of Sawré Muybu, home to about 130 indigenous Munduruku people — one in a chain of Munduruku settlements that stretch along the Tapajos River in the northern Brazilian state of Para. One small girl wears a silvery marmoset on her head as if it were a hat. A boy clutches a pet coati with a long striped tail.
Under a thatched shelter behind the chief’s house, their parents sit around a communal cooking fire. Many have fish-scale or tortoiseshell designs inked across their faces, arms and legs. A bright-green parakeet darts from shoulder to shoulder and a pet monkey chatters under a table. A few hunters with knives and bows wander in, bearing a wild boar that will be skinned, cooked and shared, eaten with yams grown in their small plantations. There are a few incongruous signs of modernity — a fridge, a satellite dish, mobile phones, a generator and a sit-on toilet — but in other ways life for these people, existing side by side with nature, has barely changed for centuries.
Any sense of an idyll, however, is shattered by a droning, throbbing hum — the unmistakable sound of a large motor. Immediately in front of the village on the river is a monstrous dredging platform, two storeys high, cobbled together Heath Robinson-style from scrap metal and parts including the landing gear of an Airbus.
Inside, four men are sifting through silt pumped up from the riverbed, which cascades down wooden ramps. They are garimpeiros — gold prospectors — looking for nuggets. The residue is made into what look like black doormats that will be taken along the river to the nearby town of Itaituba to process. The men, all from the northeast of Brazil, the poorest part of the country, dredge from dawn to dusk, for 12-14 hours, and on a good day will retrieve 20g of gold: “Da para sobreviver,” they tell me — “Enough to live on.”
The Munduruku, who number about 14,000, have the misfortune to live in the most gold-rich region in Brazil and though mining for gold in indigenous lands is illegal, the Brazilian government has no intention, it seems, to enforce the law — indeed, it is trying to change it.
“These gold-dredgers are not new. What’s new is how brazen it is — it’s a free-for-all. Before, they used to hide up channels,” says Mauricio Torres, a professor at the Federal University of Para who has been travelling in the area for 20 years, studying conflicts on indigenous lands. “The real villains are not these men but the owners outside,” he adds. “Dredges like these cost a million reals [£135,000] and are run by organised groups.”
The damage is clear to see. The dredging has turned the river, which the Munduruku consider sacred, from pale blue to muddy brown. Large sandbanks have piled up in front of the village jetty. The mercury the dredgers use to separate the gold from the sandy soil pollutes the river and contaminates their fish.
Last year a child died of mercury poisoning. Mercury has also been linked to birth defects and neurological disorders. A recent study by Brazil’s Fiocruz health institute in partnership with the World Wildlife Fund found that 58 per cent of Munduruku tested in the Tapajos River region had levels of mercury higher than that considered safe.
That’s not all the Munduruku have to contend with. To get to Sawré Muybu involved me taking two flights from Rio, an eight-hour boat trip along the Tapajos, a two-hour car journey, then two hours in a canoe. But being remote has not protected them. Illegal loggers have invaded the area. Then there is what is known locally as grilagem — land-grabbing to grow soya or rear beef cattle for the global food industry.
Brazil is the world’s biggest meat exporter. In 2016 the Munduruku narrowly avoided having their lands flooded when government plans to build a vast hydroelectric dam across the Tapajos were halted by protests. Now the government wants to construct a ferrogrão — grain railway — to transport soya to the huge port in Itaituba, from where it is exported to China and Europe.
The fate of the planet’s largest rainforest will be high on the agenda when world leaders gather in Glasgow today for the Cop26 climate change conference, which the host, Boris Johnson, has insisted must be a “turning point for humanity”. For those on the ground in the Amazon, the turning point has arrived.
“We are in a state of war,” says Cacique Juarez Saw Munduruku, 61, the village chief, his lined face furrowing. This is nothing new for the Munduruku, a warrior clan who over the centuries have fought off rival tribes and Portuguese colonialists alike, and are known as “fire ants” because of their mass assaults. Their word for stranger — pariwati — also means enemy and they once had a reputation for placing the severed heads of their adversaries on spikes.
Today their main enemy is the Brazilian government. Since the end of the military dictatorship in the 1980s, no regime has been as openly hostile towards the Munduruku and other indigenous groups as that of President Jair Bolsonaro. A former army captain, he has long contested the amount of land reserved as tribal territory. As a congressman in the late 1990s, he raged: “It’s a shame the Brazilian cavalry wasn’t as efficient as the Americans, who exterminated the Indians.”
During his presidential campaign in 2018, many of Bolsonaro’s backers were in agribusiness. He vowed that once elected, he would not designate “a single centimetre more” of land as indigenous territory, insisting the tribes had too much already.
Although the country’s constitution of 1988 guaranteed land to all Brazil’s 305 tribes and stated that indigenous territories should have all been demarcated by now, Bolsonaro’s administration has halted the process, leaving a third of indigenous land yet to be demarcated and 237 requests pending — including that of Sawré Muybu.
He has also reduced Brazil’s capacity to protect existing reserves by slashing funding to the country’s environmental agency, Ibama, and sacking thousands of government functionaries charged with monitoring them. This has emboldened those intent on plundering the forest, pushing deforestation to its highest level for 13 years, and has left indigenous communities even more vulnerable to encroachments and violent attacks.
The Sunday Times Magazine first alerted the world to the plight of the indigenous people living in the Amazon in 1969, in a cover story by the writer Norman Lewis headlined “Genocide”. That led to an international outcry and campaign. Fiona Watson, director of advocacy for Survival International, an organisation created in response to Lewis’s article to give indigenous peoples a voice on the world stage, says the situation is desperate.
“President Bolsonaro has launched the biggest assault on indigenous peoples since the military dictatorship,” she says. “The situation is without doubt the worst I’ve seen in 35 years working in Brazil and certainly the most dangerous time in decades to be indigenous, as violence against their communities is escalating and the destruction of their Amazon homeland has reached catastrophic proportions.”
Last year was the most violent to date, with a record 1,576 land disputes, according to Brazil’s Pastoral Land Commission, a church organisation that has been tracking land invasions since 1985. Almost half were against indigenous people. Few aggressors are ever brought to justice, and nowhere are there more attacks than in the state of Para.
Garimpeiros have turned particularly aggressive. In May this year, gold prospectors invaded a village in the Munduruku reserve, firing guns and setting houses on fire. One of the houses burnt to the ground belonged to the village chief and another was the home of Maria Leusa Munduruku, an indigenous leader and co-ordinator of the local women’s movement. “Please come, it’s chaos, they’re going to burn my house … They are shooting, please help me!” she cried in an audio message sent to APIB, Brazil’s largest indigenous organisation, just before communication with the village was cut off.
“They arrived with petrol in soft-drink bottles, armed and shooting,” she said afterwards. “We received phone messages saying we had to be killed because we were getting in the way, that we were denouncing their activities.”
Many of the Munduruku now leading the battle against the invaders are women. On my third morning staying with the community, sleeping in a hammock in their school room, I hear a commotion. “The warriors are back!” The shout resounds through the village, sending parrots and chickens squawking and children with painted faces scurrying.
Juarez Saw Munduruku, the village chief, and a small band of men, women and teenage boys with hair dyed green or purple, have spent the past four days armed with GPS devices as well as bows and arrows and machetes, hacking their way through dense jungle to hammer wooden signs printed with the words Terra Protegida (Protected Land) onto tree trunks on the edges of their territory.
The signs look official but are in fact copies. Though their land was mapped by Ibama in 2014 the authorities have never officially declared it a reserve, so the Munduruku have been forced into what they call self-demarcation — installing signs around the edge of all 434,900 acres of their ancestral land, as a warning to those who would plunder its riches.
Lagging behind in flip-flops, exhausted after the long hike, battling with humidity as well as the threat of venomous snakes, scorpions, spiders, even jaguars, walks a pint-sized woman dressed in a grass skirt with a headband of orange and black feathers over her long black hair. “The world talks about environment but we’re the ones whose feet are cut to pieces,” says Alessandra Korap Munduruku, 37, a mother of two boys and the tribe’s campaign co-ordinator, who tells me she will be travelling to Glasgow to alert the world to their plight. After a refreshing dip in the brook, she sits by a mango tree from which a monkey swings on a rope and explains how she became the Munduruku’s first female warrior.
“I got involved in 2015 when I attended a course on the rights of indigenous people,” she says. “I’d never thought how, when they stopped us fishing by polluting our water, they were actually taking our rights. So I joined the fight with the cacique [chief] — only I couldn’t because I am a woman and women have to stay quiet. In our society, women are married off at 12 or 13. I was lucky, as I didn’t marry till 21. My own mother said, ‘Alessandra, you can’t speak, let the cacique speak.’ I said, ‘Why not?’ I had always been a rebel and questioned everything, was always in fights. So I began to speak at meetings. To start with people were shocked but now they say, ‘Let’s wait for Alessandra to see what she thinks.’ ”
She started accompanying Cacique Juarez to Brasilia, the capital, for meetings, but soon branched out on her own. Last month she addressed the senate to warn of the impact of the proposed railway.
“I discovered many things from dealing with whites,” she says. “If they give, they always want something in return.”
She began studying law at the Federal University of Western Para after learning that two places were being offered for indigenous students. More than 500 applied but she was chosen. She has struggled to keep up with the course alongside her work organising resistance. “It’s a challenge to be a woman, to be in the struggle, to be a mum, to be a warrior — it feels as if I have the world on my shoulders,” she says.
Like Maria Leusa, she risks her life for her cause. “I am threatened like mad but I refuse to stay quiet,” she shrugs. “This is war and we must prepare for it.” In 2019, when she travelled to Brasilia with other indigenous leaders, her house was broken into and her bag and documents stolen. “Afterwards my son hugged me and said, ‘Mum, I don’t want them to kill you.’ ”
Since then she rarely stays in one place. “Why should I feel fear? The people who should feel fear are those who are doing wrong. The greatest fear I have is my people being expelled from their territory.”
Yet the war people like Alessandra are fighting is for the whole of humanity. The Amazon not only contains 10 per cent of the planet’s biodiversity but plays a vital role in mitigating climate change by acting as a sink, absorbing and storing carbon dioxide, and is often referred to as the lungs of the world. When cut or burnt down, the forest not only ceases to fulfil this function but also releases the stored carbon back into the atmosphere.
Under Bolsonaro deforestation has continued relentlessly. Between August last year and this July, 10,476 sq km of forest was wiped out — an area nearly seven times bigger than Greater London, according to data released by Imazon, a Brazilian research institute that has been tracking Amazon deforestation since 2007.
So much so that for the first time, parts of the forest are emitting more CO2 than they absorb. Scientists are warning that as much as 40 per cent of the Amazon has been so devastated that it is reaching a point of no return, at which it could switch from a rainforest to a savanna, which would have profound effects on the global climate.
“We are headed for a catastrophic temperature rise of 3-5C this century,” warned Antonio Guterres, secretary-general of the UN. “Making peace with nature is the defining task of the 21st century. It must be the top priority for everyone, everywhere.”
Bolsonaro insists he agrees. “Which other country in the world has a policy of environmental protection like ours?” he asked in his speech at the UN general assembly last month. In a way he is correct: other countries have long ago cut down their forests, whereas international alarm at the terrifying rate of Amazonian deforestation in the 1980s led Brazil to enact conservation measures and the rate slowed. But now Bolsonaro’s administration has been trying to roll back these measures. He claimed that deforestation was down in August, but shocking photos released by Greenpeace suggested otherwise.
Bolsonaro’s environment minister, Ricardo Salles, was forced to resign in June after the Brazilian supreme court announced an investigation into allegations that he and top officials in his ministry helped companies traffic illegally logged rainforest wood to Europe and the United States.
That followed the largest seizure of illegal timber in Brazil’s history — eight million cubic feet of wood — on the border between Para and Amazonas states, which police claimed they had been instructed to release.
“No one protects the forest better than indigenous people,” says Professor Torres at the University of Para. “Munduruku are the front line of resistance — particularly the women. They are preserving the forest for themselves and their children, but it has an impact for the whole world.”
Earlier this year Alessandra’s bravery was recognised with the Robert Kennedy Human Rights Award. “I never imagined I’d get a prize in my life,” she laughs. “My relatives always complained I was a troublemaker. But now they’re proud and want their daughters to be like us. In the past I walked alone, it was just me and Maria Leusa. Today there are a band of girls.”
Not only are women at the forefront but they are employing very different means from warriors of the past. Among them is Beka Munduruku, just turned 18, often referred to as the Greta of the Amazon, who posts photos on Instagram of herself and her jungle habitat. “My life used to be just playing but then I saw how they were destroying our river and home,” she says. “My people need to get our story out. Now we use WhatsApp, Facebook and Insta as weapons.”
Beka is part of a high-tech all-female team headed by Aldira, a former village teacher. While her husband looks after their four children, including a three-month-old baby, Aldira travels around with a drone, mapping deforestation and land invasions, then sends her videos to the authorities.
“They don’t do anything, but at least we register it,” she says. I watch her launch the drone over an area stripped of trees, dressed in a grass skirt and feathers, arms and legs decorated with black war paint. “If we don’t fight for the forest, who will?” she adds. “The forest gives us life and has life like us. To us, everything in the forest and river are sacred and this banditry will have consequences.”
She tells me how the Munduruku have become fearful of eating fish, once a mainstay of their diet, owing to the fear of contamination from mercury. The problem is not just the dredger.
One morning Anderson Paygo, 32, wearing a graphic T-shirt printed with the words “F*** You” over his thickly muscled arms, takes us by canoe up the river to see a goldmine. The grandson of the former chief, he is co-ordinator of 11 villages on the river, representing about 1,200 people.
“We have a lot of richness in wood, gold, even diamonds — and this government encourages people to take them,” he says.
Last year Bolsonaro introduced a draft bill in congress to allow mining and other commercial activities in indigenous territories, part of what Greenpeace has denounced as the Destruction Package. The bill is listed as one of Bolsonaro’s priorities. The National Mining Agency has received 2,899 requests to mine in indigenous territories, 1,265 in lands where there are uncontacted tribes).
Among them are 86 applications from the mining giant Anglo American, including in Munduruku land, though it is believed to have withdrawn some recently after questions were raised at a shareholders’ meeting.“Neither Anglo American nor any of its subsidiaries hold any exploration permits on indigenous lands in Brazil,” the company says. “We have withdrawn all applications for mineral exploration in areas located within indigenous lands, but several of these applications have not yet been removed from the database of the National Mining Agency (ANM).”
Some communities might lose their land altogether if a case known as Marco Temporal, or the “Time Limit Trick”, is passed by the supreme court. It follows a federal regional court ruling that it would only recognise tribal lands occupied by native communities at the time Brazil’s constitution was ratified in 1988 — which saw the territory of one tribe, the Xokleng, drastically reduced on the basis they were living on only a fraction of it.
“It feels like we are fighting grileiros [invaders] from every side,” Paygo says. “And if the government passes those laws it will be much worse. In the past our life here was very free, just hunting and fishing, but now we have to patrol our land and our leadership have to leave the village a lot to campaign. It’s not just time and effort but risk — they want the heads of me and Alessandra. But we have to do it to defend the future of our families. We don’t have fear for we are a warrior people and have always fought.”
Paygo points out a strange indentation in the trees like a ski slope — the Passage of the Wild Pigs — which he says is one of the tribe’s most sacred sites. According to their legend, the Munduruku were created by their god, Karosakaybu, born from the seed of a palm tree in Sawré Muybu. He first created fish and the river, then pigs that came down this passage to the river.
Shortly after passing it, we come to a small beach and climb out. Three scrawny men are waiting on the bank for the fortnightly supply boat. Ze, 57, Manuel and Guido, both 56, are garimpeiros from the goldmine a few miles inland. Tracks from heavy machinery mark the way towards large craters, like scars in the forest. “Six years ago there were as many as 2,000 people here with bars, shops and women,” Ze says. “Now there are just a few. There’s not much gold left.”
The garimpeiros tell us they had no idea this was indigenous land. They say they haven’t been home in two years and had no alternative but to find work here.
Two are divorced, one is separated and conditions in the jungle are grim, with frequent bouts of malaria. The supply boat comes and they load up with cooking oil, frozen chickens, a sack of corn, a long coil of sausage, tobacco and a couple of bottles of cachaça sugarcane spirit.
Not all garimpeiros are outsiders. Among those who attacked Maria Leusa were Munduruku who have turned their back on their ancient culture. The government has been trying to split the tribe, Paygo says. “Our God taught us to share, so when our people hunt and fish they always share everything, but it’s the strategy of this government to pit one family against another. Unfortunately some Munduruku joined our enemy and became garimpeiros. Some of our own family threaten us.”
Last year Bolsonaro posted a video on social media declaring: “The Indian has changed, he is evolving and becoming more and more a human being like us. What we want is to integrate him into society so he can own his land.”
Alessandra and Cacique Juarez are trying to counter this by finding new sources of income. The chief has been planting coffee and cacao. Alessandra has opened a craft store in Itaituba, a steamy Wild West town full of gold shops and brothels as well as hardware stores selling tree-cutting tools. One gold shop has a “Bar do Garimpeiro” inside, offering prospectors free drinks as their nuggets are weighed by young women in tight T-shirts and men in suits.
Some 17.7 tonnes of illegal gold entered the market from the state of Para last year, according to new figures from federal prosecutors, a third of it from garimpeiros in the Munduruku and Kayapo reserves. Some of this is believed to end up in the UK, which is the third biggest buyer of Brazilian gold.
Next to a pecking macaw, a small group of surly teenage Munduruku boys with blue-dyed hair sit smoking and playing on their phones. The chief worries that young people are losing interest in their heritage. “We chiefs are like libraries for our tribes,” he says. “In the past we didn’t have TV but they have phones and games. Our children are not interested in the old stories and are losing their language. If we lose our language and culture, what will we have? Soon the government will say these are not indigenous people, they are Brazilians like any other.”
To protect them, he is uniting with other indigenous tribes — even old enemies. “We must come together or this government will do away with all of us,” he says. “Today we’re living through a period of legislative genocide,” says Dario Kopenawa, a leader of the Yanomami people, who have seen 20,000 garimpeiros flood into their territory. “They are killing us with a pen.”
A few days after we leave, Alessandra herds 46 Munduruku onto a bus to Brasilia, a three-day journey, to take part in the country’s biggest ever demonstration by indigenous people. More than 6,000 representatives of some 176 tribes pitch tents and build bamboo shelters in which they camp for a seven-day protest titled Luta pela Vida, or Struggle for Life.
They make a striking vision dressed in their brightly coloured feathers against the gleaming white space-age buildings of congress, the supreme court and the presidential palace. Among them is Beka, live streaming to her followers.
“A lot of people still think of indigenous people as they were back in 1500, like something in a museum,” she says. “We still have our traditions but we’ve learnt to use modern ways — mobile phones, social media, speaking Portuguese — and we women are feminists. It doesn’t mean we’ve stopped being indigenous people.”

By Ben Spencer, science editor
World leaders and environmental activists from 195 countries start gathering in Glasgow today for what is billed as the “last, best chance to save the planet”. The key focus is on reducing greenhouse gas emissions, but the UK, as host of Cop26, is also pushing for an ambitious deal to halt and reverse global deforestation. Brazil, the world’s largest beef exporter, is unlikely to play ball. If the deal falters, what can the rest of us do?
Much of the food we eat either comes from or is linked to cleared land that used to be South American rainforest. Efforts to clean up the food industry have been muddied by the complexity of supply chains, particularly for processed foods such as ready meals and canned meat goods. Recent Greenpeace investigations into JBS — an international meat giant whose UK customers include several supermarkets, restaurant chains and wholesalers — found that among its suppliers were ranchers linked to deforestation. JBS insists it does not tolerate any illegal deforestation in the Amazon.
But imported meat products are only part of the problem. Soya bean, a key driver of deforestation in the Amazon, is a main source of feed for British farm animals. Three quarters of the soya imported by the UK is used as animal feed. In Europe we eat twice as much meat and three times as much dairy as the global average. The Rainforest Foundation says we can make a difference by reducing our meat intake. And when we do eat meat, we should buy from local farms with sustainable practices.
Palm oil — used in food and cosmetics — is another driver of deforestation worldwide. Read the labels on products to see if they contain palm oil and whether it comes from a sustainable source.
“Decades of inaction by governments and companies have created the crisis, emboldening the Brazilian government to further exploit the Amazon by pushing through some of the most destructive legislation ever seen,” says Anna Jones, head of forests at Greenpeace UK.
“Trusted brands still buy from forest destroyers despite promises to remove deforestation from their supply chains by 2020. Immediate action is needed on all fronts. Supermarkets must immediately drop meat suppliers owned by forest destroyers and governments must close legislative loopholes to ensure deforestation-free supply chains are exactly that.”
Brazil’s illegally mined gold also finds its way to Britain. A report published last month by the Federal University of Minas Gerais found that three countries — the UK, Switzerland and Canada — buy 72 per cent of Brazil’s gold exports. “It is very likely that those countries have imported gold linked to destructive activities in the Amazon,” the authors said. Buyers should source gold that comes from a verified low-impact mine, or buy recycled gold.

https://www.thetimes.com/world/article/j.title: Judge recommends Makah tribe can resume whaling
https://www.thetimes.com/world/article/j.text:
The last time members of the Makah tribe killed a whale their village in northwest Washington state erupted in celebrations while animal rights protesters and the operators of several whale-watching boats staged protests as the creature was dragged to the shore.
Now, after years in which further hunts have been held up by legal challenges, the tribe may be allowed to kill once again, upon the recommendation of a judge who found that it would have little impact on a populace of gray whales at least 21,000 strong.
“It’s thousands of years of tradition for us,” TJ Greene, chairman of the Makah Tribal Council, said. “Our oral history teaches us that [whaling] was given to us early in our history.”
The tribe’s reservation has only small rivers, without “that abundance of salmon that other tribes had along the coast”, he said. For at least 2,000 years they relied on “marine mammals and halibut”.
In 1855 when the tribe signed a treaty with the US government, ceding 300,000 acres of land, it retained “the right of taking fish and of whaling or sealing at usual and accustomed grounds”.
In the 1920s when the depletion of whales from commercial fishing became apparent to the tribe, it stopped whaling, Greene said. Then, in May 1999, it staged a new hunt.
“I was there when the whale was brought in,” Greene said. “There were thirteen hundred people on the beach; it was packed, elbow to elbow, to watch the carcass come in.”
Other tribes had sent canoes that hooked up to the whale to help pull it to shore. A machine to lift the carcass above the waterline was not strong enough, so logs were laid on the beach and ropes attached to the creature, and “hundreds of people that were down there all pulled in unison”, he said. “It was really a special moment.”
But after the hunt animal rights activists filed a legal challenge and a judge concluded that the Makah should seek a waiver under the 1972 Marine Mammal Protection Act. “It’s been 17 or 18 years in this process,” Greene said.
In a legal brief arguing for the waiver, the tribe lamented that a new generation of Makahs had been born and some elders had died. “The hunt brought great benefits to Makahs in the form of fresh meat and blubber, the ability to perform songs, dances and ceremonies, and a level of community cohesiveness few living Makahs had previously experienced.”
Now George Jordan, an administrative law judge in Seattle, has recommended that the Makah be granted a waiver allowing the tribe to kill three eastern North Pacific gray whales on even years and one of the whales on an odd year — a schedule timed with regard to the migratory patterns of the western North Pacific gray whale, which is far rarer.
The decision over whether the tribe will now be allowed to resume the hunts falls to the National Marine Fisheries Service. Greene said whale hunts may be allowed to begin next spring, though he suspects it will take longer. “This practice and this vocation is part of both our spiritual and ceremonial practices that define us,” he said. “That’s the real hard part for us, that they are regulating that part of our belief system.”
A representative for Greenpeace USA has said the tribe ought to be able to exercise its treaty rights. But the Animal Welfare Institute remains staunchly opposed to the Makah’s resumption of whaling. “All gray whales face critical anthropogenic threats from climate change, ocean noise, oil and gas development, pollution, coastal developments, contaminants, bycatch and ship strikes,” it said in a statement.
It added that it supported “tribal sovereignty” and respected the tribe’s traditions as they were expressed “through stories, art and dance”. But it argued that “hunting these animals is biologically insupportable”.
