https://www.thetimes.com/culture/tv-radi.title: Greg Wise: ‘When my wife saw my first dance she burst into tears’
https://www.thetimes.com/culture/tv-radi.text:
Of course, there is one question for actor Greg Wise that looms above all others: what on earth did he do with the condoms Emma Thompson gave him?
“Oh God, oh no, must we?” he says. “Really? I mean, it was a joke, the only way my wife could reasonably respond to the famous curse!”
Wise is, of course, talking about Strictly Come Dancing, in which he is appearing at the moment. And the curse refers to the litany of previous contestants who have run off with their dance partners.
It was double Oscar-winning Thompson who encouraged her reluctant husband to accept the Strictly challenge in the first place. Feeling confident that their 18-year marriage could survive a rumba with another woman, she packed him off with a couple of condoms. Ribbed, flavoured, king-size? He won’t say.
“The condoms gave Karen [Hauer, his dance partner] a good laugh and then — if you really want to know — I gave them to my son, Tindy,” he admits, finally.
Wise is sitting in his kitchen at home in Hampstead, north London. Thompson is in the background. He has just returned from Strictly rehearsals at Elstree Studios in which he performed the paso doble as James Bond for the show’s movie night.
“It was hard because being 007 and a matador well . . . they’re quite different,” he says, opening a beer. Thompson brings him another one from the fridge. She hasn’t noticed that he has already helped himself.
“What a woman!” he enthuses. “A wife who brings you a beer when you’ve already got one — that’s love and commitment, isn’t it?”
Wise is very genial company. He takes nothing about himself or his work too seriously. “I think it’s important to have a light touch,” he says. “Although that isn’t a reason not to give something your all. My friend Bill Bailey [the comedian who won Strictly last year] gave me some good advice. He said doing it was ‘top japes’, but you have to do the work if you’re going to get anything out of it. And he was right. It’s physically demanding. Bill had terrible blisters by the end, but so far I’m fine. No aches, no pains, nothing.”
What about the mental toll? The singer Sophie Ellis-Bextor (who was on the show in 2013) recently described how her husband needed counselling to deal with the insecurities that her appearance provoked.
“Em and I haven’t experienced anything like that,” Wise says. “As for the pressure of performing, if you did think about it too much you’d dissolve into tears. It’s like being asked to start learning Bulgarian on Monday — with an address to the nation in Bulgarian booked for Saturday.”
Wise doesn’t speak Bulgarian. He doesn’t rate his dancing skills much higher.
“Mrs Wise [Thompson] has been very encouraging and helpful,” he says. “She got me to do a bit of stretch before dancing, which I was previously a bit sniffy about. And I’ve had my reward.”
What does that mean?
“When she saw a video of my first dance she burst into tears. It was very emotional. She had no idea her old man could pull off something like this.”
Wise, though, had another, very particular reason for appearing on the show. His older sister, Clare, died of bone cancer in 2016. During her illness she wrote a blog that Wise continued after her death and eventually published as a book, Not That Kind of Love. Clare loved dancing — she was even buried in a glitterball coffin — and he says that she would have insisted that he took part.
“People keep asking if she’d be proud; actually I think she’d be thrilled and bemused,” Wise says. “But the most rewarding thing for me is using my Strictly opportunity to speak about end-of-life in a mature way. I want to drag the conversation out of the dark spaces. I mean, we British are still so adolescent about death, aren’t we? I’ve had the privilege of meeting the author Kathryn Mannix. She wrote a book called With the End in Mind, which powerfully makes the point: we all have two days with less than 24 hours in them during our lives — the day we are born and the day we die. Societal gaze is focused on the first, and yet we can learn so much by acknowledging how unpredictable and finite life is. I know acknowledging that with Clare enriched me no end.”
In the final months of her life Wise moved in with his sister to provide her care (she lived on the same street in north London). His account of her final days, her final moments even, is extraordinarily powerful. There is more to come.
Wise is on the second draft of a new book about what he learnt from the experience. “Trauma and grief can provoke great change in someone,” he says. “It doesn’t have to be crippling or detrimental. Caring for Clare made me kinder, more empathetic and careful as a person. It’s a terrible, terrible thing to say, but I am a much improved human being as a result of the death of my sister. It’s a terrible, terrible thing to say, but it’s true.”
He sounds as though he’s being quite tough on himself. I know many women who think Wise represents the high point of modern masculinity. He’s easy on the eye, thoughtful, funny, but also brave and kind.
And then there is all the appealing outdoorsy stuff. When his wife is away filming, Wise clears off to their cottage on the shore of Loch Eck in Argyll. It’s down a muddy track with no internet and no television. Wise forages, chops down trees and carves presents for family and friends from wood. He’s in bed at 9pm and up at 4.30am for a wash in the river.
“That’s where I most want to be,” he says. “Me and Em managed to sneak there for six days at the end of August. We caught and smoked some mackerel. We collected ten kilograms of porcini mushrooms. Ten kilos! Unheard of! The whole house stinks of them now.”
However, you mustn’t tell Wise that he is the perfect man because that might “imbalance the universe”.
“We have to stop this right now, OK? All this ‘oh, he’s lovely in every way’. It’s nonsense. The universe is balanced and there are two sides to everyone. Do you know, very early on in our relationship Emma actually said to me, ‘You really must get in touch with your dark side. You just can’t be nice and empathetic the whole time.’ And I did. I have done a tremendous amount of therapy. I reached inside my innards to find out about myself, and it’s the best, most rewarding work I’ve ever done.”
Wise and his sister grew up in Northumberland with their architect mother and architect professor father. It wasn’t a happy marriage and it took him years of talking to unravel its impact.
“It was a middle-class household, there was food on the table, but a very difficult emotional landscape to exist in,” he says. “Clare and I took completely different things away from it. She never had a romantic attachment in her whole life [she was 51 when she died]. I absolutely require a romantic attachment to survive.”
At weekends he and Thompson are cooking, talking and reading. Their 21-year-old daughter, Gaia, and adopted son, Tindy, 33, are often around too. Famously Wise has not watched TV for 35 years.
“We’ve taken London friends up to the cottage in Scotland and they fall apart,” he says. “There is no sound and no ambient life after dark. I get quite feral. I feel completely in tune with nature.”
The off-grid lifestyle has a political dimension. In 2019 Thompson was criticised for attending an Extinction Rebellion demonstration in London (she had taken a flight from Los Angeles days before). Would Wise be annoyed if the Extinction Rebellion affiliate Insulate Britain blocked his car on the way home from Strictly?
“Oh God, look, we are in deep shit, aren’t we? We have to do something about the planet. If people are prepared to queue for four hours for petrol, then perhaps they should get out of their cars and chat to protesters who are rightfully terrified about what is happening. That’s my daughter’s generation. When the waters rise and we’re all forced to move further up the hill, we’ll certainly have the conversation then, won’t we?”
